The XYZ Affair. A diplomatic scandal that brought America to the brink of war with France and rallied the young nation around a principle: it would not be bullied.

In 1797, President John Adams sent three envoys to Paris to negotiate. The goal was simple: settle trade disputes and do something about French seizures of American merchant ships. The United States needed peace with France.

The French Foreign Minister Charles Maurice de Talleyrand sent three intermediaries to meet with the American envoys. These intermediaries were not there to negotiate in good faith. They had one job: demand a bribe.

The French wanted two hundred and fifty thousand French livres, roughly fifty thousand dollars. They also demanded a ten million dollar loan to France. Only after America paid these demands would the French be willing to discuss actual negotiations. It was extortion, pure and simple.

The American envoys refused. They had no authority to pay bribes, and they weren't going to start. They reported the extortion back to President Adams.

Adams then made a bold decision. He published the dispatches, the official records of what the French had done. But he concealed the identities of the three intermediaries. Instead of their real names, he used the letters X, Y, and Z. Hence the name: the XYZ Affair.

The American public exploded in outrage. This was an insult to national honor. France thought it could treat young America like a weak nation and extort money. Americans rallied around a phrase that captured their fury: "Millions for defense, not one cent for tribute."

The scandal pushed America toward armed conflict. The Quasi-War began, an undeclared naval conflict between the United States and France that lasted from 1798 to 1800. It damaged Franco-American relations for years.

Things began to improve after Napoleon took power in 1799. Diplomatic negotiation resumed. The Convention of 1800 formally ended the hostilities. But the scandal had shown something significant about the young American nation. It demonstrated that even though America was young and small, it could resist foreign coercion. The affair helped cement national unity around principles of sovereignty and honor. John Adams was the president who exposed the extortion and rallied public opinion. Charles Maurice de Talleyrand orchestrated the bribe scheme. And the scandal revealed what the early United States would and would not accept from the great powers of Europe.
